# Conversion Review
<!-- Slide 4 -->

## Which Constructor Converts? {.smaller}

~~~cpp
Fahrenheit(double value = 32.0) { degrees = value; }
Fahrenheit(const Temperature& t) { degrees = t * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0; }
~~~

- Tuesday's two `Fahrenheit` constructors. Which one converts?

::: notes
Slides 5–9

Give students a few seconds to commit. Most will pick the Temperature constructor, because that is the one the slide called a conversion on Tuesday.
:::

<!-- Slide 5 -->

---

## Both of Them

~~~cpp
Fahrenheit oops = 20.0;
cout << oops.value() << endl;
~~~

. . .

- Output: `20`, meaning 20 degrees Fahrenheit, not Celsius.
- Any constructor that is not `explicit` and takes one value converts.
- The fix: `explicit Fahrenheit(double value = 32.0)`

::: notes
Tested with g++. With explicit, Fahrenheit oops = 20.0; fails with "conversion from 'double' to non-scalar type 'Fahrenheit' requested." Fahrenheit b; and Fahrenheit f(20.0); still compile, because explicit does not block direct initialization.

The Temperature constructor stays implicit: Fahrenheit names the unit and nothing is lost. A bare 20.0 does not say which unit it is, so that constructor fails the test.
:::

<!-- Slide 6 -->

---

## Lightning Review

::: {.incremental}
- What does `explicit` block?
  - Implicit conversions in copy initialization, argument passing, and return. Not direct initialization such as `Fahrenheit f(20.0);`
- How is a conversion operator written?
  - `operator double() const`, with no return type and no parameters.
- When is an implicit conversion safe?
  - When the target type names the meaning and nothing is lost.
- Why can't `Temperature` become `Fahrenheit` by way of `double`?
  - That route needs two user-defined conversions, and the compiler never chains two.
:::

::: notes
Ask each question aloud and give students a few seconds before revealing the answer. The last question answers why Fahrenheit(double) never fires when a Temperature is converted.
:::

<!-- Slide 7 -->

---

## Used, Not Kept

~~~cpp
Fahrenheit(const Temperature& t) { degrees = t * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0; }
~~~

- The constructor reads `t` and keeps only a `double`.
- Using an object without storing it is a dependency, from 05.02.
- The rest of today: classes that keep other objects as members.

::: notes
05.02 defined a dependency as class A using class B temporarily, with B not stored in A. Fahrenheit depends on Temperature only while the constructor runs.
:::

<!-- Slide 8 -->

---

## Summary

- Any constructor that is not `explicit` and takes one value is a conversion; mark the ones you do not intend `explicit`.
- Using an object without storing it is a dependency; the rest of today is about classes that store objects.

::: notes

:::
